title: Modern British and European History
topics: Cold War, decolonisation and European integration

notes.h: Approaches to history: from Ranke to the cultural turn
notes.body:
Historiography is the study of how history has been written: the methods, assumptions and debates that shape interpretations. Exam answers improve sharply when you name the school behind a reading and explain why it reaches its conclusions.

- Rankean empiricism: Leopold von Ranke (1795–1886) professionalised history around archival research and source criticism, aiming to show the past as it actually was. G.R. Elton's The Practice of History (1967) defended this tradition.
- E.H. Carr, What is History? (1961): facts do not speak for themselves; the historian selects them, so we should study the historian before the history.
- Whig history: Herbert Butterfield's The Whig Interpretation of History (1931) attacked reading the past as steady progress towards the present.
- Marxist history and history from below: E.P. Thompson's The Making of the English Working Class (1963) treated class as a lived experience and sought to rescue ordinary people from the condescension of posterity. Eric Hobsbawm framed the long nineteenth century around a 'dual revolution' (French political, British industrial).
- The Annales school: Marc Bloch and Lucien Febvre founded the journal in 1929; Fernand Braudel's The Mediterranean (1949) layered time into the longue durée, social and economic conjunctures, and the short-lived history of events.
- The linguistic and cultural turns: Hayden White's Metahistory (1973) argued that historical writing follows literary forms of emplotment. Richard Evans's In Defence of History (1997) replied that evidence still constrains interpretation.
- Gender and postcolonial history: Joan Scott's 1986 article made gender 'a useful category of historical analysis'; Edward Said's Orientalism (1978) showed how Western knowledge about the 'East' was bound up with power.

Applied illustration: on the origins of the Holocaust, intentionalists stress Hitler's long-held aims, while functionalists (structuralists) stress chaotic decision-making and radicalisation from below. Saying which camp a historian belongs to, and what evidence each favours, is worth more than a list of names.

Source skills: judge provenance (who wrote it, when, why, for whom), typicality and silences. A Cabinet minute and a diary answer different questions; neither is simply 'biased' or 'reliable'.

Common pitfalls:
- Treating historiography as a list of names rather than a set of arguments about method and evidence.
- Setting up a crude 'Carr against Elton' contest without noting how much they shared.
- Calling postmodernists relativists who deny the past existed; most argue about representation, not reality.
- Forgetting that a school's questions shape its answers (Annales historians largely ignored high politics by design).

notes.h: Britain 1815–1914: reform, industry and the liberal state
notes.body:
Britain avoided revolution in this period while transforming its economy, franchise and state. Explaining why is a classic exam theme.

Post-war tension and early reform:
- The Corn Law of 1815 protected landed interests. Peterloo (Manchester, 1819) saw cavalry charge a reform meeting, followed by the repressive Six Acts.
- Catholic Emancipation (1829) split the Tories. The Great Reform Act of 1832 abolished many rotten boroughs, gave seats to industrial towns and set a uniform £10 household franchise in the boroughs. Even so, only around one adult man in five in England and Wales could vote.
- Whig social legislation followed: the Factory Act 1833 (with inspectors), abolition of slavery in most of the empire (1833) and the Poor Law Amendment Act 1834, which built workhouses on the principle of 'less eligibility'.

Chartism and free trade:
- The People's Charter (1838) had six points, including universal male suffrage and the secret ballot. Mass petitions failed in 1839, 1842 and 1848.
- Peel's repeal of the Corn Laws (1846) split the Conservatives and made free trade a near-consensus. The Great Exhibition (1851) symbolised mid-Victorian confidence; W.L. Burn called the 1850s–60s an 'age of equipoise'.

Extending the franchise:
- Second Reform Act 1867 (Disraeli): household suffrage in the boroughs, roughly doubling the electorate.
- Ballot Act 1872; Corrupt and Illegal Practices Act 1883.
- Third Reform Act 1884 extended household suffrage to the counties; the 1885 Redistribution Act created mostly single-member seats.

Late Victorian and Edwardian politics: Gladstone's Home Rule Bills (1886, 1893) split the Liberals and failed. After 1906 the New Liberals passed Old Age Pensions (1908) and the National Insurance Act (1911). The Lords' rejection of the 1909 People's Budget led to the Parliament Act 1911, which replaced the Lords' veto with a suspensory delay.

Industry: the 'standard of living' debate sets optimists (such as R.M. Hartwell) against pessimists (such as Hobsbawm). Revisionist work since the 1980s, notably by N.F.R. Crafts, presents industrialisation as more gradual than older accounts of a sudden take-off.

Illustration: why no revolution in 1848? Answers point to the 1832 settlement absorbing the middle classes, repeal easing food prices, railway-era prosperity, firm policing of the Kennington Common meeting, and the moderation of many Chartists.

Common pitfalls:
- Calling 1832 'democratic'. It strengthened property as the basis of the vote.
- Presenting reform as Whig inevitability. Party advantage (Disraeli in 1867) mattered.
- Treating Chartism as a total failure. Five of its six points were later achieved.

notes.h: Revolutions and nationalism in nineteenth-century Europe
notes.body:
After 1815 the Vienna settlement tried to contain liberalism and nationalism. By 1871 nationalism had remade the map, though usually through states and armies rather than popular revolution.

The Vienna order:
- The Congress of Vienna (1814–15) restored legitimate dynasties, balanced the powers and created the German Confederation under Austrian presidency. The Concert of Europe managed crises through conferences.
- Metternich's Carlsbad Decrees (1819) imposed censorship and surveillance on universities.
- The 1830 revolutions brought the July Monarchy in France and Belgian independence.

1848: revolutions broke out in Paris (February), Vienna and Berlin (March) and across Italy. The Frankfurt Parliament offered the imperial crown to Frederick William IV of Prussia, who refused it in 1849. Reasons for failure:
- Divisions between liberals and radicals, and middle-class fear of social revolution after the Paris June Days.
- Rival nationalisms, for example Germans against Czechs and Magyars against Croats.
- Armies stayed loyal to their rulers. Lewis Namier called 1848 a 'revolution of the intellectuals'.

Italian unification:
- Mazzini's Young Italy stood for republican nationalism; Cavour, Piedmont's prime minister, relied on diplomacy.
- The Plombières agreement (1858) brought French help in the 1859 war against Austria, and Piedmont gained Lombardy.
- Garibaldi's Thousand took Sicily and Naples (1860). The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861, Venetia followed in 1866 and Rome in 1870.

German unification:
- The Zollverein (1834) built Prussian economic leadership. Bismarck became minister-president in 1862 and promised 'blood and iron'.
- Three wars followed: Denmark (1864), Austria (1866, Königgrätz) and France (1870–71). The Empire was proclaimed at Versailles on 18 January 1871.
- Historians debate whether Bismarck followed a master plan or improvised skilfully, and whether economics (the Zollverein) did more than diplomacy.

Theories of nationalism:
- Modernists: Ernest Gellner (1983) linked nationalism to industrial society's need for a shared high culture. Benedict Anderson's Imagined Communities (1983) stressed print capitalism. Hobsbawm and Ranger edited The Invention of Tradition (1983).
- Ethno-symbolists: Anthony D. Smith argued that nations build on older ethnic myths and symbols.
- Miroslav Hroch described three phases of national movements: scholarly interest, patriotic agitation and mass movement.
- Eugen Weber's Peasants into Frenchmen (1976) argued that rural France was only nationalised between 1870 and 1914.

Common pitfalls:
- Treating unification as the fulfilment of popular nationalism. Both were largely 'revolutions from above'.
- Ignoring international context: the Crimean War left Austria isolated and Russia estranged from it and unwilling to uphold the 1815 order, while France misjudged Prussia.
- Calling 1848 a total failure. Serfdom was abolished in Austria and Prussia gained a constitution.

From about 1880 the 'New Imperialism' saw European powers carve up most of Africa and much of Asia and the Pacific. The central exam question is why, and historians disagree sharply.

Key events:
- The Indian Rebellion of 1857 led to Crown rule (Government of India Act 1858). Victoria became Empress of India in 1876.
- Disraeli bought Suez Canal Company shares (1875); Britain occupied Egypt in 1882.
- The Berlin Conference (1884–85) set rules for claiming African territory. It did not itself partition Africa.
- Leopold II's Congo Free State was notorious for forced labour and atrocities in the rubber trade; Belgium annexed it in 1908.
- Britain and France confronted each other at Fashoda (1898).
- In the South African War (1899–1902) British concentration camps caused the deaths of many thousands of Boer and African civilians.
- German forces committed genocide against the Herero and Nama in South West Africa (1904–08).

Explanations:
- Economic: J.A. Hobson, Imperialism: A Study (1902), blamed surplus capital and underconsumption at home. Lenin's Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (1917) linked empire to monopoly finance capital.
- Peripheral: Gallagher and Robinson's 'The Imperialism of Free Trade' (1953) argued Britain preferred informal influence and annexed only when that failed. Africa and the Victorians (1961) traced the 'official mind' and crises on the periphery, notably Egypt. Robinson later stressed the role of local collaborators.
- Gentlemanly capitalism: Cain and Hopkins (1993) located the driving force in the City of London and services rather than industry.
- Strategic and political: the security of routes to India, great-power prestige, and domestic politics (Bismarck's colonial turn in 1884–85).
- Cultural: Social Darwinism, missionary humanitarianism and Said's Orientalism.

Imperial culture at home: John MacKenzie's Propaganda and Empire (1984) found empire saturating popular culture. Bernard Porter's The Absent-Minded Imperialists (2004) argued many Britons were largely indifferent. J.R. Seeley's 1883 remark that Britain acquired its empire in a fit of absence of mind is often misread as a celebration, when it was really a call for Britons to think about empire seriously.

Illustration: Egypt 1882 tests the theories. Bondholders' interests support Hobson and Cain and Hopkins. The Urabi revolt and the Canal route support Gallagher and Robinson. A strong answer weighs both.

Common pitfalls:
- Treating the Berlin Conference as the moment Africa was divided.
- Applying one theory to every empire and every decade.
- Leaving out African and Asian agency: resistance, collaboration and negotiation shaped the outcome.
- Moralising without analysis. Judgement should come from evidence.

notes.h: The First World War: origins, conduct and peace
notes.body:
Origins:
- Long-term: the alliance system (Dual Alliance 1879, Triple Alliance 1882, Franco-Russian alliance 1894, Entente Cordiale 1904, Anglo-Russian Convention 1907), the Anglo-German naval race after HMS Dreadnought (1906), Balkan instability (the Bosnian crisis of 1908, the Balkan Wars of 1912–13) and rigid mobilisation plans.
- July Crisis: Franz Ferdinand was assassinated at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. Germany gave Austria-Hungary the 'blank cheque', the ultimatum went to Serbia on 23 July, and Austria declared war on 28 July. Germany declared war on Russia (1 August) and France (3 August). Britain entered on 4 August after Germany invaded Belgium under the Schlieffen Plan.

Historiography of origins:
- Article 231 of the Versailles Treaty assigned responsibility to Germany and its allies. Interwar opinion then drifted towards shared responsibility.
- Fritz Fischer's Griff nach der Weltmacht (1961) argued Germany pursued aggressive, expansionist war aims and bore the main responsibility. His Krieg der Illusionen (War of Illusions, 1969) added that elites sought war partly to escape domestic pressures (the primacy of domestic politics).
- Christopher Clark's The Sleepwalkers (2012) spread responsibility across all the powers' decision-makers. Critics say this underplays Berlin and Vienna.

Conduct: the Marne (September 1914) stopped the German advance and trench deadlock followed. Verdun (1916) and the Somme (from 1 July 1916, when the British suffered about 57,000 casualties on the first day) became bywords for attrition, followed by Passchendaele (1917). Russia left after the 1917 revolutions (Brest-Litovsk, March 1918), and the US entered in April 1917. Germany's Spring Offensive (March 1918) failed, and the Allied Hundred Days, beginning at Amiens on 8 August, led to the Armistice of 11 November 1918.

Generalship debate: Alan Clark's The Donkeys (1961) popularised 'lions led by donkeys'. Revisionists such as John Terraine and Gary Sheffield (Forgotten Victory, 2001) argue that a 'learning curve' in artillery, all-arms tactics and logistics produced victory in 1918.

Total war and the home front: in Britain the Defence of the Realm Act (1914), conscription (Military Service Act 1916), state control of munitions and a growing female workforce. The Representation of the People Act 1918 enfranchised all men over 21 and women over 30 who met a property qualification.

The peace: the Treaty of Versailles (signed 28 June 1919) took Alsace-Lorraine and the colonies, limited the army to 100,000 men, demilitarised the Rhineland and imposed reparations. Keynes's The Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919) condemned it as Carthaginian. Margaret MacMillan's Peacemakers (2001) and Sally Marks defend the peacemakers' constraints and stress that reparations were less crushing in practice than claimed.

Common pitfalls:
- Blaming 'the alliances' mechanically. Italy did not join its allies in 1914.
- Treating the Somme only as futility without considering its attritional effect on the German army.
- Treating Versailles as the direct cause of the Second World War.

The interwar years combined economic crisis with the collapse of democracies and the rise of new regimes claiming total control over society.

Soviet Union:
- The Bolsheviks seized power in October 1917, won the Civil War and retreated into the New Economic Policy (1921).
- Stalin's 'revolution from above' brought the Five-Year Plans (from 1928) and forced collectivisation, which produced famine in 1932–33, devastating in Ukraine (the Holodomor) and Kazakhstan.
- The Great Terror (1936–38) saw mass arrests and executions.

Italy: Mussolini was appointed prime minister after the March on Rome (October 1922). After the murder of the socialist deputy Matteotti (1924), the dictatorship was consolidated in 1925–26.

Germany:
- Weimar survived hyperinflation (1923) and stabilised under the Dawes Plan (1924), but the Depression after the Wall Street Crash (October 1929) proved fatal.
- Presidential cabinets governed by Article 48 decree. The Nazis became the largest party in July 1932, and Hitler was appointed chancellor on 30 January 1933 through a deal among conservative elites.
- The Reichstag fire decree (February 1933), the Enabling Act (March 1933), the Night of the Long Knives (1934) and the Nuremberg Laws (1935) followed.

The totalitarian model: Hannah Arendt's The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951) stressed terror and ideology. Friedrich and Brzezinski (1956) listed six features: an official ideology, a single mass party, terror, a monopoly of communications, a monopoly of weapons and central economic control. Critics argue the model overstates monolithic control:
- Martin Broszat and Hans Mommsen described the Nazi state as polycratic; Mommsen called Hitler a 'weak dictator'.
- Ian Kershaw's concept of 'working towards the Führer' explains how officials radicalised policy by anticipating Hitler's wishes.
- Sheila Fitzpatrick's social history of Stalinism looked at participation and upward mobility from below.

Britain and appeasement: Britain faced the General Strike (1926) and the 1931 crisis that produced the National Government. The League failed over Manchuria (1931) and Abyssinia (1935). Then came the Rhineland (1936), the Anschluss (March 1938), Munich (September 1938), Prague (March 1939) and the Nazi–Soviet Pact (23 August 1939).
- Guilty Men (1940) condemned the appeasers.
- Revisionists stress economic, imperial and military constraints and the strength of public opinion.
- R.A.C. Parker (1993) argued Chamberlain had real alternatives, such as an earlier alliance with France and the USSR, and rejected them.

Common pitfalls:
- Saying Hitler was 'elected' dictator. He never won a majority in a free election.
- Using 'totalitarian' as a mere label without engaging with its critics.
- Judging appeasement with hindsight of 1939–45.

notes.h: The Second World War: conduct, genocide and the home front
notes.body:
Course of the war:
- Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939; Britain and France declared war on 3 September. The 'Phoney War' ended in spring 1940 with Norway and then the fall of France (May–June). Dunkirk evacuated the BEF.
- The Battle of Britain (summer–autumn 1940) prevented invasion, and the Blitz followed.
- Operation Barbarossa (22 June 1941) opened the Eastern Front, where most German land forces fought and died. Pearl Harbor (7 December 1941) brought the US in; Hitler declared war on the US on 11 December.
- Turning points in 1942–43: Midway (June 1942), El Alamein (October–November 1942), Stalingrad (German surrender, February 1943), Kursk (July 1943) and Allied success in the Battle of the Atlantic (May 1943).
- D-Day (6 June 1944) and the Soviet Operation Bagration (June 1944) crushed Germany between two fronts. Germany surrendered in May 1945 (VE Day, 8 May). After the atomic bombings of Hiroshima (6 August) and Nagasaki (9 August), Japan surrendered on 15 August and signed on 2 September 1945.

Why the Allies won: Richard Overy's Why the Allies Won (1995) argues that superior resources were not enough by themselves; Allied victory also depended on production organisation, technology, morale and leadership, and the Soviet recovery was decisive. Adam Tooze's The Wages of Destruction (2006) shows Germany's economic weakness relative to the Allies.

The Holocaust: about six million Jews were murdered. Persecution escalated from the Nuremberg Laws to Kristallnacht (1938), ghettoisation in Poland, mass shootings by the Einsatzgruppen after Barbarossa, and death camps (Operation Reinhard; Auschwitz-Birkenau). The Wannsee Conference (20 January 1942) coordinated implementation rather than first deciding on genocide.
- Intentionalists, such as Lucy Dawidowicz (1975), emphasise Hitler's ideology and planning.
- Functionalists, such as Broszat and Mommsen, emphasise cumulative radicalisation within a chaotic state.
- Christopher Browning's Ordinary Men (1992) explained perpetrators through conformity, deference and situational pressure. Daniel Goldhagen (1996) blamed 'eliminationist antisemitism' in German culture, and most specialists criticised his argument.

British home front: evacuation, rationing and the Emergency Powers Acts. The Beveridge Report (1942) identified five 'giants' (Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor, Idleness). Angus Calder's The People's War (1969) and The Myth of the Blitz (1991) questioned the image of unbroken unity. Historians still debate whether the war created a post-war consensus.

Diplomacy: Tehran (1943), Yalta (February 1945) and Potsdam (July–August 1945) shaped the post-war settlement and the division of Germany.

Common pitfalls:
- Writing an Anglo-centric narrative that ignores the Eastern Front.
- Saying the Holocaust was 'decided at Wannsee'.
- Treating intentionalism and functionalism as mutually exclusive. Most historians now synthesise them (Kershaw, Longerich).

notes.h: Cold War, decolonisation and European integration
notes.body:
Cold War:
- Churchill's 'iron curtain' speech (March 1946), the Truman Doctrine (March 1947) and the Marshall Plan (1947) were followed by the Berlin Blockade (1948–49) and NATO (1949).
- The USSR tested an atomic bomb in 1949, and the Korean War (1950–53) militarised containment.
- Hungary was crushed (1956), the Berlin Wall built (1961), the Cuban Missile Crisis followed (October 1962), and the Warsaw Pact invaded Czechoslovakia (1968).
- Détente produced the Helsinki Final Act (1975). Gorbachev (from 1985), the fall of the Berlin Wall (9 November 1989), German reunification (3 October 1990) and the dissolution of the USSR (December 1991) ended the conflict.

Origins debate:
- Orthodox accounts blamed Soviet expansionism.
- Revisionists, such as William Appleman Williams (1959) and Gabriel Kolko, stressed American economic expansion.
- Post-revisionists, led by John Lewis Gaddis, blended the two. After the Soviet archives opened, Gaddis's We Now Know (1997) put more weight on Stalin.
- Geir Lundestad described the US presence in Western Europe as an 'empire by invitation'.

Decolonisation:
- India and Pakistan became independent in August 1947 amid the violence of Partition. Britain withdrew from Palestine in 1948.
- Counter-insurgency in Malaya (1948–60) and Kenya (Mau Mau, 1952–60) involved detention and abuse, documented by Caroline Elkins (2005) and the 'migrated archives' disclosed during the Mutua litigation (2011). The government settled with Kenyan claimants in 2013.
- Suez (1956) exposed British dependence on the US. Ghana became independent in 1957, and Macmillan gave his 'wind of change' speech in 1960.
- France lost Indochina (Dien Bien Phu, 1954) and fought a brutal war in Algeria (1954–62). The Belgian Congo became independent in 1960 and fell into crisis.
- John Darwin and others weigh metropolitan, international (US, UN, Cold War) and peripheral (nationalist) causes.

European integration:
- The Schuman Declaration (9 May 1950) led to the ECSC (Treaty of Paris, 1951). The European Defence Community failed in 1954, and the Treaty of Rome (1957) created the EEC.
- De Gaulle vetoed British entry in 1963 and 1967. The UK joined in 1973 and voted to stay in the 1975 referendum.
- The Single European Act (1986) and Maastricht (1992) deepened integration. The UK voted to leave in 2016 and left on 31 January 2020.
- Interpretations: federalist idealism; Alan Milward's The European Rescue of the Nation-State (1992), which argued integration served national welfare goals; and Andrew Moravcsik's liberal intergovernmentalism (1998).

Illustration: Britain stayed out in 1950–57 because of Commonwealth trade, the 'three circles' world role and suspicion of supranationalism.

Common pitfalls:
- Writing Cold War history only from Washington and Moscow.
- Presenting decolonisation as orderly and voluntary.
- Calling the EEC simply a peace project and ignoring economic interests.

cards.f: What is historiography?
cards.b: The study of how history has been written: the methods, assumptions, sources and debates behind historical interpretations.

cards.f: What was Leopold von Ranke's contribution to the discipline?
cards.b: He professionalised history around archival research and critical evaluation of sources, aiming to reconstruct the past as it actually happened.

cards.f: Central claim of E.H. Carr's What is History? (1961)?
cards.b: Facts do not speak for themselves. Historians select and interpret them, so readers should study the historian before the history.

cards.f: Who wrote The Practice of History (1967), and what did it defend?
cards.b: G.R. Elton. It defended rigorous empirical, archive-based method against Carr's relativism and against theory-driven history.

cards.f: What is 'Whig history', and who named the critique?
cards.b: Reading the past as steady progress towards the present, judging actors by whether they advanced it. Herbert Butterfield criticised it in 1931.

cards.f: Explain Braudel's three levels of historical time.
cards.b: The longue durée (slow geographical and environmental structures), conjunctures (medium-term social and economic cycles) and l'histoire événementielle (short-term events).

cards.f: What did E.P. Thompson mean by class as a 'happening'?
cards.b: Class is not a fixed structure but something people make through shared experience and consciousness, as in The Making of the English Working Class (1963).

cards.f: What was Hayden White's argument in Metahistory (1973)?
cards.b: Historical narratives follow literary modes of emplotment (romance, tragedy, comedy, satire), so form shapes meaning as much as evidence does.

cards.f: How did Richard Evans respond to postmodernism?
cards.b: In Defence of History (1997) accepted that interpretation is unavoidable but insisted that evidence constrains it and that some accounts are demonstrably better than others.

cards.f: What did Joan Scott argue in 1986?
cards.b: That gender, the socially constructed relations between the sexes, is a 'useful category of historical analysis' for understanding power, not just a matter of adding women to the story.

cards.f: What did the Great Reform Act of 1832 change?
cards.b: It removed many rotten boroughs, gave seats to industrial towns, and set a uniform £10 household franchise in the boroughs, while keeping property as the basis of the vote.

cards.f: What happened at Peterloo (1819)?
cards.b: Cavalry and yeomanry charged a large reform meeting at St Peter's Field, Manchester, killing and wounding many. The government responded with the repressive Six Acts.

cards.f: Name three of the six points of the People's Charter (1838).
cards.b: Any three of: universal male suffrage, secret ballot, no property qualification for MPs, payment of MPs, equal constituencies, annual parliaments.

cards.f: Why did Peel's repeal of the Corn Laws (1846) matter politically?
cards.b: It split the Conservative Party, with the Peelites leaving the protectionists, and made free trade a lasting national orthodoxy.

cards.f: What was the principle of 'less eligibility' in the 1834 Poor Law?
cards.b: Relief in the workhouse had to be less attractive than the lowest independent labour, to deter the able-bodied from claiming.

cards.f: Why did Disraeli pass the Second Reform Act (1867)?
cards.b: Partly to 'dish the Whigs' and win credit for the Conservatives. Accepting radical amendments produced borough household suffrage and roughly doubled the electorate.

cards.f: What did the Parliament Act 1911 do?
cards.b: It ended the Lords' veto over money bills and replaced its veto on other bills with a suspensory delay, following the Lords' rejection of the 1909 People's Budget.

cards.f: Two key New Liberal welfare measures before 1914?
cards.b: Old Age Pensions (1908) and the National Insurance Act (1911), which covered sickness and some unemployment.

cards.f: What is the 'standard of living debate'?
cards.b: The argument over whether early industrialisation raised or lowered working-class living standards. Optimists (e.g. Hartwell) say raised; pessimists (e.g. Hobsbawm) say lowered or stagnant.

cards.f: What did the Third Reform Act (1884) and Redistribution Act (1885) achieve together?
cards.b: They extended household suffrage to the counties and created mostly single-member constituencies of more equal size.

cards.f: Name three aims of the Vienna settlement of 1814–15.
cards.b: Restore legitimate dynasties, build a balance of power that contained France, and manage disputes through the Concert of Europe.

cards.f: What were the Carlsbad Decrees (1819)?
cards.b: Measures driven by Metternich that imposed censorship, university surveillance and the suppression of nationalist student societies across the German Confederation.

cards.f: Why did the Frankfurt Parliament fail?
cards.b: Liberals were divided over the borders of Germany, the parliament had no army, and Frederick William IV refused the crown in 1849 as Austria and Prussia regained control.

cards.f: Give three reasons the 1848 revolutions failed.
cards.b: Liberal–radical splits and fear of social revolution, competing nationalisms such as Magyar against Croat, and armies that stayed loyal to their rulers.

cards.f: Compare Mazzini and Cavour.
cards.b: Mazzini wanted a democratic republic made by popular insurrection. Cavour pursued Piedmontese expansion through diplomacy and French help.

cards.f: What was agreed at Plombières (1858)?
cards.b: A secret deal in which Napoleon III promised French military support against Austria in exchange for Nice and Savoy.

cards.f: List Bismarck's three wars of unification.
cards.b: Against Denmark (1864), Austria (1866, decided at Königgrätz) and France (1870–71). The German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles in January 1871.

cards.f: How did Benedict Anderson explain nationalism?
cards.b: Nations are 'imagined communities'. Print capitalism let strangers imagine themselves as members of one nation.

cards.f: Contrast modernist and ethno-symbolist theories of the nation.
cards.b: Modernists (Gellner, Anderson) see nations as products of modernity. Ethno-symbolists (Anthony D. Smith) argue they build on pre-modern ethnic myths and symbols.

cards.f: What is Hroch's three-phase model?
cards.b: National movements pass from scholarly interest (Phase A) through patriotic agitation (Phase B) to a mass movement (Phase C).

cards.f: What was the Berlin Conference (1884–85)?
cards.b: A meeting of powers that set rules for claiming African territory, such as 'effective occupation' of coasts, and recognised Leopold II's Congo. It did not itself partition Africa.

cards.f: Hobson's explanation of imperialism (1902)?
cards.b: Underconsumption at home created surplus capital, and financiers pushed for empire to secure profitable investment outlets.

cards.f: How did Lenin's theory differ from Hobson's?
cards.b: Lenin saw imperialism as an inevitable stage of monopoly finance capitalism leading to war between rivals. Hobson thought domestic reform could remove the cause.

cards.f: What is the 'imperialism of free trade'?
cards.b: Gallagher and Robinson's 1953 argument that Britain preferred informal influence and annexed territory only when informal means failed.

cards.f: What is 'gentlemanly capitalism'?
cards.b: Cain and Hopkins's thesis that the City of London, finance and services, rather than industrialists, drove British imperial expansion.

cards.f: Why did Britain occupy Egypt in 1882?
cards.b: To protect the Suez route and European bondholders after the Urabi revolt threatened the Khedive's regime and Anglo-French financial control.

cards.f: What happened at Fashoda in 1898?
cards.b: A French expedition met Kitchener's force on the Upper Nile. France backed down, and the episode came to symbolise Anglo-French rivalry in Africa.

cards.f: What was the outcome of the Indian Rebellion of 1857?
cards.b: East India Company rule ended and the Government of India Act 1858 transferred India to direct Crown rule.

cards.f: MacKenzie v Porter on imperial culture?
cards.b: MacKenzie (1984) found empire saturating British popular culture. Porter (2004) argued many Britons were largely indifferent to it ('absent-minded imperialists').

cards.f: What did Edward Said argue in Orientalism (1978)?
cards.b: Western scholarship and art built an image of the 'Orient' as backward and exotic, and this knowledge supported imperial domination.

cards.f: What was the 'blank cheque'?
cards.b: Germany's promise in early July 1914 to support Austria-Hungary unconditionally in dealing with Serbia after Sarajevo.

cards.f: Why did Britain enter the war on 4 August 1914?
cards.b: Germany invaded Belgium, whose neutrality Britain had guaranteed in 1839. Strategic commitment to France and fear of German dominance also mattered.

cards.f: What was the Fischer thesis?
cards.b: Fritz Fischer (1961) argued that Germany pursued expansionist war aims and bore the main responsibility, partly to deal with domestic political pressures.

cards.f: What is Christopher Clark's argument in The Sleepwalkers (2012)?
cards.b: War came from interlocking decisions by many governments, none of them fully foreseeing the result, so responsibility is shared rather than mainly German.

cards.f: What is the 'learning curve' debate?
cards.b: Revisionists such as Sheffield argue the BEF improved its artillery, tactics and logistics enough to win in 1918, against the 'lions led by donkeys' view.

cards.f: What was the Schlieffen Plan?
cards.b: A German plan to defeat France quickly through Belgium before turning east against Russia. Its failure at the Marne produced stalemate.

cards.f: Significance of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (March 1918)?
cards.b: Bolshevik Russia left the war and ceded huge territories, freeing German divisions for the Spring Offensive in the West.

cards.f: What did the Representation of the People Act 1918 do?
cards.b: It gave the vote to all men over 21 and to women over 30 who met a property qualification, nearly tripling the electorate.

cards.f: What was Keynes's critique of Versailles?
cards.b: In The Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919) he called it a Carthaginian peace whose reparations would ruin Germany and destabilise Europe's economy.

cards.f: Name three military terms imposed on Germany at Versailles.
cards.b: An army limited to 100,000 men, no conscription, no tanks or military aircraft, and a demilitarised Rhineland (any three).

cards.f: What were the six features of totalitarianism for Friedrich and Brzezinski (1956)?
cards.b: Official ideology, a single mass party, terror, a monopoly of communications, a monopoly of weapons and central control of the economy.

cards.f: What does 'working towards the Führer' mean?
cards.b: Ian Kershaw's term for how officials radicalised policy by anticipating Hitler's wishes, which reconciles Hitler's centrality with the chaos of the Nazi state.

cards.f: What was the Enabling Act (March 1933)?
cards.b: A law allowing the Hitler cabinet to legislate without the Reichstag, the legal basis of the dictatorship.

cards.f: How did Hitler become chancellor?
cards.b: Through appointment by Hindenburg on 30 January 1933, after conservative elites around von Papen believed they could control him. He did not win a majority.

cards.f: What was Article 48 of the Weimar constitution?
cards.b: The emergency power letting the president rule by decree. It was used heavily by presidential cabinets from 1930.

cards.f: What was Stalin's 'revolution from above'?
cards.b: Rapid industrialisation through Five-Year Plans from 1928, plus forced collectivisation, transforming the USSR at enormous human cost.

cards.f: What was the Holodomor?
cards.b: The 1932–33 famine in Soviet Ukraine caused by collectivisation and grain requisitioning. Many states recognise it as genocide.

cards.f: What did Mommsen mean by Hitler as a 'weak dictator'?
cards.b: Hitler avoided routine decisions and let agencies compete, so policy emerged from polycratic rivalry rather than a coherent plan.

cards.f: What was agreed at Munich (September 1938)?
cards.b: Britain, France and Italy agreed with Germany that the Sudetenland would be transferred from Czechoslovakia. Czechoslovakia was not represented at the conference.

cards.f: R.A.C. Parker's position on appeasement?
cards.b: A counter-revisionist view: Chamberlain had alternatives, such as a firm alliance with France and the USSR, but chose to pursue appeasement.

cards.f: What was Operation Barbarossa?
cards.b: The German invasion of the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941, opening the Eastern Front where the bulk of German forces were destroyed.

cards.f: Why was Stalingrad a turning point?
cards.b: The German Sixth Army surrendered in February 1943, ending the run of German offensive success in the East and boosting Soviet morale.

cards.f: What was the purpose of the Wannsee Conference (20 January 1942)?
cards.b: To coordinate the bureaucratic implementation of the 'Final Solution' across agencies. It did not make the initial decision for genocide.

cards.f: Intentionalism v functionalism on the Holocaust?
cards.b: Intentionalists stress Hitler's ideology and long-term aims. Functionalists stress cumulative radicalisation in a chaotic, polycratic state.

cards.f: What did Browning's Ordinary Men (1992) argue?
cards.b: Members of Reserve Police Battalion 101 killed mainly through conformity, deference to authority and situational pressure, not through unique ideological fanaticism.

cards.f: What are Overy's main explanations for Allied victory?
cards.b: Effective organisation of production, technology, morale and leadership, plus Soviet recovery, rather than just superior raw resources.

cards.f: The five 'giants' of the Beveridge Report (1942)?
cards.b: Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness.

cards.f: What was argued in Calder's The Myth of the Blitz (1991)?
cards.b: The image of united, cheerful Britons was partly a constructed myth that hid looting, class tension and low morale.

cards.f: Why was the Battle of the Atlantic crucial?
cards.b: Britain's survival and the build-up for D-Day depended on Atlantic convoys. Victory over the U-boats by mid-1943 secured supply lines.

cards.f: What was decided at Yalta (February 1945)?
cards.b: Germany's division into occupation zones, Soviet entry into the war against Japan, a promise of free elections in liberated Europe, and plans for the founding conference of the United Nations.

cards.f: What was the Truman Doctrine (1947)?
cards.b: A US pledge to support free peoples resisting subjugation, launched with aid to Greece and Turkey. It marked the start of containment.

cards.f: Orthodox, revisionist and post-revisionist views on Cold War origins?
cards.b: Orthodox: Soviet expansionism caused it. Revisionist: US economic expansion caused it. Post-revisionist: misperception and security dilemmas on both sides.

cards.f: What is 'empire by invitation'?
cards.b: Geir Lundestad's argument that West Europeans actively sought American involvement and protection after 1945.

cards.f: Why was Suez (1956) significant for Britain?
cards.b: US financial pressure forced Britain and France to withdraw, exposing British dependence on Washington and limits on its independent power.

cards.f: What was Macmillan's 'wind of change' speech?
cards.b: A 1960 speech in Cape Town acknowledging the strength of African nationalism and signalling faster British decolonisation.

cards.f: What did the 'migrated archives' reveal?
cards.b: Files removed from colonies at independence, disclosed in 2011 during the Mau Mau litigation, documented abuse and the deliberate destruction of records.

cards.f: What did the Schuman Declaration (1950) propose?
cards.b: Pooling French and German coal and steel under a supranational High Authority, making war between them materially impossible. It led to the ECSC (1951).

cards.f: What was Milward's thesis on European integration?
cards.b: Integration rescued the nation-state: governments pooled sovereignty to deliver national economic and welfare goals, not to transcend the nation.

cards.f: Why did de Gaulle veto British EEC entry in 1963?
cards.b: He saw Britain as too tied to the US and the Commonwealth, and as a threat to French leadership of the Community.

cards.f: What was the Brezhnev Doctrine?
cards.b: The claim after the 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia that socialist states could intervene when socialism was threatened in a fellow socialist country.

questions.q: Which historian wrote What is History? (1961), arguing that the historian selects and shapes the facts?
questions.why: Carr's 1961 lectures argued that facts become historical only when historians select them. Elton replied in The Practice of History (1967).

questions.q: Which measure set a uniform £10 household franchise in the parliamentary boroughs?
questions.why: The 1832 Act created the £10 borough householder qualification. The 1867 Act later moved to household suffrage in the boroughs.

questions.q: Which statement about the Frankfurt Parliament is correct?
options: It unified Germany under Austrian leadership in 1849
It offered the imperial crown to Frederick William IV, who refused it
It was dissolved by Bismarck in 1862
It led directly to the creation of the Zollverein
questions.why: In 1849 the parliament offered Frederick William IV of Prussia the crown of a 'Little German' empire. He refused a crown offered by an elected assembly.

questions.q: Gallagher and Robinson's 'imperialism of free trade' (1953) argues that:
options: Britain annexed territory mainly to find markets for surplus manufactures
Imperialism was the highest stage of monopoly capitalism
Britain preferred informal influence and annexed territory only when that failed
City financiers were the main drivers of empire
questions.why: Their thesis stresses continuity between informal and formal empire: Britain preferred informal influence and annexed only when that failed. 'Highest stage of monopoly capitalism' is Lenin, and putting City financiers at the centre is Cain and Hopkins's gentlemanly capitalism.

questions.q: What immediately triggered Britain's declaration of war on Germany on 4 August 1914?
options: Germany's declaration of war on Russia
questions.why: Britain had guaranteed Belgian neutrality in 1839, and the German advance through Belgium decided the Cabinet. The Lusitania was sunk in 1915.

questions.q: Which concept did Ian Kershaw use to explain how Nazi policy radicalised without detailed orders from Hitler?
questions.why: Kershaw's phrase describes officials anticipating Hitler's wishes. Cumulative radicalisation is Mommsen's term, and polycracy describes the competing agencies.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects current scholarship on the Wannsee Conference (20 January 1942)?
options: It was where Hitler personally ordered the extermination of European Jews
It coordinated the implementation of a genocide whose mass killing had already begun
It decided to deport Jews to Madagascar
It was a meeting of the Allied powers to discuss war crimes
questions.why: Mass shootings in the occupied USSR and gassing at Chełmno had already begun. Wannsee organised cooperation across agencies under Heydrich.

questions.q: Alan Milward's The European Rescue of the Nation-State (1992) argued that European integration:
options: Was driven mainly by federalist idealists aiming to abolish the nation-state
Was imposed by the United States through the Marshall Plan
Allowed national governments to pursue domestic economic and welfare goals
Was primarily a response to the Soviet nuclear threat
questions.why: Milward argued that pooling sovereignty strengthened post-war nation-states by helping them deliver prosperity and welfare.

questions.q: Which Chartist demand had NOT been achieved by 1918?
options: Abolition of the property qualification for MPs
questions.why: The secret ballot came in 1872, the property qualification was abolished in 1858 and MPs were paid from 1911. Annual parliaments were never adopted.

questions.q: On what date was Hitler appointed Chancellor of Germany?
questions.why: Hindenburg appointed him on 30 January 1933. In August 1934, after Hindenburg's death, Hitler merged the offices of chancellor and president.

questions.q: Explain two differences between the Rankean empiricist tradition and the Annales school.
markScheme: Rankeans focus on political, diplomatic and state history; Annales on social, economic and environmental structures
Rankeans privilege the short-term narrative of events; Annales prefers the longue durée and conjunctures
Rankeans rely on close criticism of official archival documents; Annales draws on geography, demography, economics and other disciplines
Develops each difference with a named example (e.g. Ranke or Elton contrasted with Braudel's Mediterranean)
questions.modelAnswer: The Rankean tradition, later defended by Elton, centred on states, diplomacy and politics, rebuilt through close criticism of archival documents. The Annales historians, from Bloch and Febvre in 1929 onwards, turned to society, economy and mentalities. First, they changed the timescale: Braudel's Mediterranean (1949) placed slow geographical structures and economic cycles above the 'surface' of events. Second, they changed the method by drawing on geography, demography and statistics rather than relying mainly on state papers.

questions.q: Assess briefly why Britain avoided revolution in 1848.
markScheme: The 1832 Act brought the middle classes into the political nation, separating them from working-class radicals
Repeal of the Corn Laws (1846) and recovery after 1848 reduced economic distress
Firm state preparation for the Kennington Common meeting (10 April 1848): special constables and troops
Divisions within Chartism (moral force against physical force) and a petition discredited by false signatures
Contrast with the Continent, where liberal and national grievances combined with weak or divided regimes
Reaches a supported judgement on the most important factor
questions.modelAnswer: The most important factor was the 1832 settlement. By admitting much of the propertied middle class, it split them from working-class radicals, unlike Paris or Vienna where liberals joined the revolution. Repeal in 1846 eased the politics of bread, and the state prepared carefully for Kennington Common with special constables and troops. Chartism was also divided, and the 1848 petition was ridiculed over false signatures. Britain had no national grievance comparable to the Italians' or Hungarians', so 1848 tested a regime that was already flexible.

questions.q: Outline two ways in which Bismarck's diplomacy contributed to German unification.
markScheme: Isolated Austria by securing Russian goodwill and French neutrality before 1866 (e.g. Biarritz, 1865)
Allied with Italy (1866) to open a second front against Austria
Lenient peace with Austria at Prague (1866) to avoid lasting enmity
Used the Ems Telegram (1870) to provoke France into declaring war, bringing the southern states in
questions.modelAnswer: First, Bismarck isolated Austria before 1866. He cultivated Russia, sounded out Napoleon III at Biarritz in 1865, and allied with Italy so that Austria would face a war on two fronts. Second, he made France appear the aggressor in 1870. His edited Ems Telegram provoked a French declaration of war, which activated the southern states' defensive alliances with Prussia and produced the national enthusiasm that carried them into the Empire in 1871.

questions.q: Using the British occupation of Egypt (1882), explain one strength and one weakness of the 'gentlemanly capitalism' thesis.
markScheme: Strength: Egypt's debt crisis and the Dual Control show City and bondholder interests at stake
Develops the strength: Cain and Hopkins link occupation to protecting finance and services
Weakness: Gallagher and Robinson stress strategic anxiety over the Suez route and the local crisis of the Urabi revolt
Develops the weakness: Gladstone's government was reluctant and expected a temporary occupation, which suggests strategic reasons rather than City lobbying
questions.modelAnswer: Strength: Egypt's bankruptcy in 1876 led to Anglo-French financial control. Bondholders, many in London, had much to lose if the Urabi movement repudiated the debt, which fits Cain and Hopkins's emphasis on finance. Weakness: the decision-makers talked mainly about the Suez route to India and the collapse of order. Gladstone, who had denounced imperial adventures, occupied Egypt reluctantly and promised withdrawal. Gallagher and Robinson's focus on the official mind and crises on the periphery explains that hesitation better.

questions.q: Explain why the Fischer thesis caused such controversy in West Germany in the 1960s.
markScheme: Challenged the interwar consensus of shared responsibility and revived Article 231
Suggested continuity in German expansionist aims from 1914 to 1939, implicating more than Hitler
Used German archival evidence such as the September Programme (1914)
Located causes in the domestic elites' fear of socialism, unsettling conservative national history
questions.modelAnswer: Fischer used German archives, including Bethmann Hollweg's September Programme of 1914, to argue that Germany's leaders pursued sweeping expansionist aims. This overturned the comfortable view that all the powers had slid into war together. It also implied continuity between Wilhelmine Germany and Hitler, so Nazism looked less like an aberration. By linking war to elites' fear of socialism at home, it challenged the conservative historical establishment, led by Gerhard Ritter.

questions.q: Identify two factors that explain the Nazi rise to power between 1929 and 1933.
markScheme: The Depression: mass unemployment and the discrediting of Weimar parties
Effective propaganda and organisation appealing across classes, especially to the Protestant middle classes and rural voters
Breakdown of parliamentary government: rule by Article 48 decree from 1930
Backstairs intrigue by conservative elites (Papen, Hindenburg's circle) who appointed Hitler
questions.modelAnswer: The Depression was fundamental. Unemployment reached around six million by early 1932, and the moderate parties were discredited, so Nazi support rose from 2.6% in 1928 to 37.3% in July 1932. But votes alone did not bring Hitler to office. After 1930 parliament was sidelined by Article 48 decrees, and conservatives around Papen persuaded Hindenburg to appoint Hitler in January 1933, believing they could contain him.

questions.q: Give two reasons why the Eastern Front was decisive in the defeat of Nazi Germany.
markScheme: The majority of German army casualties occurred in the East
Soviet victories (Stalingrad, Kursk) broke German offensive capacity before D-Day
Operation Bagration (June 1944) destroyed Army Group Centre at the same time as D-Day
Soviet industrial recovery after relocating factories east of the Urals
questions.modelAnswer: First, the East absorbed and destroyed most of the German army. Most German military deaths occurred there, and Stalingrad (February 1943) and Kursk (July 1943) ended Germany's capacity for strategic offensives. Second, in summer 1944 Operation Bagration destroyed Army Group Centre while the Western Allies fought in Normandy. Germany was crushed between two fronts, and the Soviet effort meant D-Day faced a weakened enemy.

questions.q: Explain three factors behind the acceleration of British decolonisation after 1956.
markScheme: Suez exposed British weakness and dependence on US goodwill
Rising nationalist movements (e.g. Gold Coast and Nkrumah; Kenya) raised the cost of control
Economic reassessment: Macmillan's 1957 cost–benefit audit of colonies and the growing pull of Europe
International pressure from the US and the UN, and Cold War fears of driving nationalists towards communism
The Hola Camp scandal (1959) undermined the moral case for colonial rule
Iain Macleod as Colonial Secretary (1959–61) speeded up timetables
questions.modelAnswer: Suez in 1956 showed that Britain could not act against US wishes, which weakened the will to hold on by force. Nationalist movements raised the costs of control. Ghana's independence in 1957 set an example, and the Hola Camp killings in Kenya in 1959 discredited coercion at home. Economic thinking also changed: Macmillan commissioned an audit of the colonies' value and turned towards Europe. Under Iain Macleod, independence timetables in Africa shortened sharply, as signalled in the 1960 'wind of change' speech.

questions.q: How far does the 'learning curve' interpretation rehabilitate the British high command on the Western Front?
markScheme: States the thesis: the BEF developed effective artillery, all-arms tactics and logistics by 1918 (Sheffield, Terraine)
Evidence: creeping barrages, counter-battery fire, platoon tactics and success in the Hundred Days
Limitation: learning came at enormous cost (Somme, Passchendaele), and some failures were avoidable
Limitation: credit may belong to junior officers, technology and munitions output rather than Haig
Reaches a balanced judgement (it rehabilitates the army more than individual commanders)
questions.modelAnswer: The learning curve shows that the BEF of 1918 was a sophisticated force. Predicted artillery fire, counter-battery work, tanks, aircraft and flexible platoon tactics won the Hundred Days. This undermines the 'donkeys' caricature. Yet it does not clear the commanders. Passchendaele was continued long after its aims had become unrealistic, and Haig repeatedly expected a breakthrough. Much of the learning came from junior officers and from munitions output. The thesis rehabilitates the army as an institution more than it rehabilitates its leaders.

questions.q: A historian describes a British colonial governor's report of 1920 as 'biased and therefore useless'. Explain why this judgement is flawed.
markScheme: Bias does not make a source useless; utility depends on the question asked
The report is highly useful for official attitudes, assumptions and the 'official mind'
Read against the grain, it can reveal resistance or local agency that the author tried to minimise
Must be evaluated through provenance, purpose and audience, and corroborated with other sources
questions.modelAnswer: Every source has a perspective, so 'biased' is not a reason to discard one. Usefulness depends on the question. For how colonial officials saw their subjects, the governor's report is first-rate evidence. Read against the grain, it can also reveal what it tries to play down, such as protests or local intermediaries. The historian should analyse its provenance, purpose and audience, perhaps Whitehall superiors, and corroborate its claims with other sources.

questions.q: 'Historians cannot escape their own time, so objectivity is an illusion.' Discuss with reference to at least two schools of historical thought.
markScheme: Defines objectivity and distinguishes complete neutrality from disciplined, evidence-based judgement
Carr: the historian's selection of facts reflects present concerns
Postmodern and linguistic turn: White on emplotment; narrative form shapes meaning
Marxist history: Thompson's political commitments shaped his questions but produced lasting scholarship
Empiricist response: Elton on archival discipline; Evans on evidence constraining interpretation
Uses an example of a debate shifting with its era (e.g. the Fischer controversy or Cold War origins after archives opened)
Distinguishes the influence of the present on questions from its influence on answers
Reaches a supported conclusion (e.g. objectivity as a regulative ideal rather than an achieved state)
questions.modelAnswer:
The proposition is half right. Historians cannot achieve a view from nowhere, but it does not follow that all interpretations are equally valid.

Carr argued in 1961 that the historian chooses which facts become 'historical', and that choice reflects present concerns. The point is easy to illustrate. Cold War revisionism flourished during Vietnam, and E.P. Thompson's history from below grew out of his socialist politics. Hayden White pushed further, claiming that historians impose literary plots on the past, so that form shapes meaning before evidence is weighed.

Yet the history of these debates also shows that evidence can discipline interpretation. Thompson's political commitments led him to new questions, but his findings about artisans' radicalism were tested in the archives and largely survived. Fischer's thesis came out of a West German reckoning with the past, but it stood or fell on documents such as the September Programme. When the Soviet archives opened, Gaddis revised Cold War interpretations towards stressing Stalin, which shows that new evidence changes conclusions. Elton and later Evans argued that source criticism, footnotes and peer scrutiny let historians reject demonstrably false accounts, as the courts did when they rejected David Irving's distortions in the 2000 libel case.

The key distinction is between questions and answers. The present shapes which questions historians ask: gender history emerged with feminism, and postcolonial history with decolonisation. Answers, though, remain answerable to evidence. Objectivity is therefore best understood as a regulative ideal: an aim pursued through transparent method, not a state of neutrality any historian reaches. To call it an illusion confuses the impossibility of perfect detachment with the impossibility of better and worse history.

questions.q: 'The extension of the franchise between 1832 and 1884 owed more to party advantage than to popular pressure.' How far do you agree?
markScheme: 1832: Whig fear of disorder (Reform Bill riots, Days of May) together with a desire to secure the propertied classes
Chartism (1838–48) failed in the short term, showing the limits of popular pressure
1867: Disraeli's competition with Gladstone and acceptance of radical amendments (Hodgkinson)
1867: the Reform League and the Hyde Park railings episode (1866) as pressure from below
1884: Gladstone's Liberal advantage in the counties; deal with Salisbury over redistribution (1885)
Changing ideas: Gladstone's 1864 'pale of the constitution' speech; the respectable artisan
Distinguishes timing (party) from underlying causes (social change, pressure)
Supported overall judgement across the whole period
questions.modelAnswer:
Party advantage determined the form and timing of reform, but popular pressure and social change explain why the question kept returning.

In 1832 the Whigs acted partly from conviction and partly from fear. The Reform Bill riots in Bristol and Nottingham and the Days of May in 1832 convinced Grey that reform would prevent revolution. Yet the design was conservative. The £10 franchise brought in the propertied middle class and left working men outside, which suggests that elite strategy shaped the outcome.

Chartism shows the limits of pressure alone. Three mass petitions in 1839, 1842 and 1848 were rejected outright, because no party gained from accepting them.

1867 is the strongest case for party advantage. Disraeli seized the issue after Russell and Gladstone's bill failed in 1866, and he accepted amendments such as Hodgkinson's to outbid the Liberals and keep control of the Commons. The result, household suffrage in the boroughs, went further than either leadership wanted. But the Reform League's agitation, including the Hyde Park demonstration of 1866, created the atmosphere in which reform seemed unavoidable. Gladstone's 1864 claim that respectable working men belonged within the 'pale of the constitution' reflected a changed view of the artisan.

In 1884 Gladstone extended the vote to the counties partly because rural householders were expected to vote Liberal. The Lords forced a compromise, and Salisbury extracted single-member seats in 1885 that helped Conservatives in the suburbs. Here bargaining between parties is plain, with little mass agitation.

Overall, the statement is largely right about the immediate causes, especially in 1867 and 1884. Yet parties competed over the franchise only because industrialisation, urban growth and organised working-class respectability had made the question unavoidable. Popular pressure set the agenda, and party advantage decided the terms.

questions.q: 'German unification was achieved by coal and iron rather than blood and iron.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explains Keynes's later paraphrase versus Bismarck's 1862 'blood and iron' speech
Zollverein (1834) excluded Austria and built Prussian economic leadership
Prussian industrial growth (Ruhr coal, railways, Krupp) funded army reform (Roon, Moltke)
Military victories: 1864, Königgrätz (1866), Sedan (1870) were decisive
Bismarck's diplomacy isolated each opponent (Russia, France, Italy)
Limits of economics: southern states in the Zollverein still voted anti-Prussian in the 1868 Customs Parliament elections
International context: Crimean War left Austria isolated; French miscalculation in 1870
Reaches a judgement integrating economic preconditions with political and military agency
questions.modelAnswer:
The phrase, usually traced to Keynes, inverts Bismarck's 1862 claim that the great questions of the day would be settled by blood and iron. The best answer treats coal and iron as necessary preconditions, and blood, iron and diplomacy as the decisive means.

Economic arguments are strong. The Zollverein, founded in 1834, tied the German states' trade to Prussia while excluding Austria, whose protectionist industries could not join. From the 1850s Prussia's coal, iron and railway boom, centred on the Ruhr and Silesia, funded Roon's army reforms. Railways let Moltke mobilise faster than Austria in 1866 and France in 1870, and Krupp's steel artillery was decisive at Sedan.

Yet economics did not produce political unity on its own. In the 1868 Customs Parliament elections, southern voters returned many anti-Prussian deputies, which shows that economic integration had not created a desire for Prussian leadership. Bavaria and Württemberg joined the Empire only after the war of 1870 generated national feeling against France.

Political agency was therefore crucial. Bismarck isolated each enemy in turn. Austria was drawn into the Danish war and then out-manoeuvred; Russia's goodwill was secured; and Italy became an ally in 1866. In 1870 the Ems Telegram made France the apparent aggressor. The lenient Peace of Prague kept Austria out of the war of 1870. International conditions also helped: Austria had alienated Russia during the Crimean War, and Napoleon III misjudged Prussia.

Unification was therefore achieved by blood and iron, built on coal and iron. The economic base made Prussian military supremacy possible. But the particular outcome, a 'Little German' empire under Prussia proclaimed at Versailles, came from war and diplomacy that could have gone differently, as Königgrätz nearly did.

questions.q: 'The Scramble for Africa is best explained by events in Africa rather than in Europe.' Assess this view.
markScheme: Explains the peripheral or excentric thesis (Gallagher and Robinson; Robinson on collaboration)
Egypt 1882 as the trigger in Africa and the Victorians: crisis on the periphery prompting rivalry
Local agents: Rhodes, the Royal Niger Company, Leopold's agents and French officers in West Africa
Collapse of collaborative systems (e.g. the Urabi revolt, the expansionist Asante or Ndebele states)
European explanations: Hobson and Lenin (capital), Cain and Hopkins (City finance)
Great-power politics: Bismarck's 1884–85 colonial bid, French search for prestige after 1871
Technology (quinine, steamships, Maxim gun) made conquest cheap: enabling rather than motivating
Supported judgement on the interaction between metropole and periphery
questions.modelAnswer:
The periphery explains where and when the Scramble began. Europe explains why it became a competitive rush rather than a series of local crises.

Gallagher and Robinson argued in Africa and the Victorians (1961) that Britain's 'official mind' was drawn in reluctantly by crises on the ground. The occupation of Egypt in 1882 followed the Urabi revolt's challenge to the Khedive and Anglo-French financial control. It alienated France and set off rivalry elsewhere. Robinson's later theory of collaboration explained annexation as a response to the breakdown of local partners. Men on the spot also forced the pace: Rhodes's British South Africa Company, Goldie's Royal Niger Company and French officers advancing from Senegal often acted ahead of their governments.

Yet a purely peripheral account struggles to explain why the rush was so fast and so general after 1880. Bismarck's sudden colonial claims in 1884–85, in Togo, Cameroon, South West Africa and East Africa, reflected European diplomacy and German domestic politics rather than African crises. France sought prestige after 1871. Leopold II's private ambition, pursued through European diplomacy, produced the Congo Free State. Hobson and Lenin emphasised the search for investment outlets, and Cain and Hopkins the needs of London finance. These theories fit southern Africa's gold better than they fit tropical Africa, where little capital went.

Technology mattered too. Quinine, steamers and the Maxim gun made conquest cheap. They explain capacity rather than motive.

The proposition overstates the case. African developments, including resistance and the collapse of intermediaries, created the openings. European rivalry, intensified by German unification and an anxious balance of power, turned scattered crises into a general partition. The Scramble is best explained as the interaction between the two.

questions.q: 'Germany bears the main responsibility for the outbreak of war in 1914.' Discuss with reference to the historiography.
markScheme: Article 231 and the 1919 verdict; interwar revisionism and Lloyd George's 'slithered' view
Fischer (1961): German war aims, the September Programme, the 'War Council' of December 1912 (contested)
The blank cheque (5–6 July 1914) and German pressure on Vienna to act quickly
Austria-Hungary's own agency: Conrad and Berchtold's determination to crush Serbia
Russia's early mobilisation measures (from 25 July; general mobilisation 30 July) and French support (Poincaré's visit)
Clark's Sleepwalkers: shared responsibility, Serbian context and the Black Hand
Critics of Clark (e.g. Annika Mombauer) reaffirming German and Austrian primacy
Supported judgement distinguishing localised war from continental war
questions.modelAnswer:
Germany bears the main, though not the sole, responsibility for turning a Balkan crisis into a continental war.

The Versailles verdict of 1919 gave way in the interwar years to Lloyd George's view that the nations 'slithered' into war. Fritz Fischer revived German responsibility in 1961. He used documents such as Bethmann Hollweg's September Programme to show sweeping war aims, and he highlighted the so-called War Council of December 1912, though historians dispute its significance.

The July Crisis supports much of Fischer's case. On 5–6 July Germany gave Austria-Hungary unconditional backing and urged rapid action, accepting the risk that Russia would intervene. Berlin calculated that war in 1914 was preferable to war later, against a Russia whose railways and army were expanding. The Schlieffen Plan also meant that any war with Russia would involve an immediate attack on France through Belgium, which brought Britain in.

Christopher Clark's The Sleepwalkers broadens the view. Serbian officials tolerated the Black Hand, Austria-Hungary was determined to crush Serbia on its own account, and Russia began pre-mobilisation measures on 25–26 July and ordered general mobilisation on 30 July, before Germany. Poincaré's visit to St Petersburg strengthened the alliance's resolve. Critics, among them Annika Mombauer, reply that only Berlin and Vienna wanted a war of some kind in July 1914, while others acted in response.

The most persuasive judgement distinguishes levels. Austria-Hungary chose a local war against Serbia. Germany encouraged it knowing it might become general, and its war plan guaranteed that a war in the east would also be a war in the west. Russia and France made the escalation easier but did not seek it. 'Main responsibility' therefore rests on Germany, with Austria-Hungary close behind, even if Clark rightly warns against a single-culprit story.

questions.q: 'The concept of totalitarianism obscures more than it reveals about Nazi Germany and Stalin's Soviet Union.' Discuss.
markScheme: Defines the concept: Arendt (1951) on ideology and terror; Friedrich and Brzezinski's six-point syndrome (1956)
Notes its Cold War context and political uses
Strengths: captures unprecedented ambitions for total control, mass mobilisation, terror and camps; enables comparison
Weaknesses for Nazism: polycracy (Broszat), the 'weak dictator' (Mommsen), private business and the churches
Weaknesses for Stalinism: Fitzpatrick's social history, popular participation and denunciation, regional chaos in the Terror
Different ideologies and aims: racial empire versus class-based modernisation
Post-1990 revival: archives show both centrally directed terror and initiative from below; Kershaw's 'working towards the Führer'
Distinguishes the concept as an ideal type from the claim that regimes achieved total control
Comparative frameworks (Kershaw and Lewin, Stalinism and Nazism: Dictatorships in Comparison, 1997)
Sustained, nuanced judgement
questions.modelAnswer:
Used as a description of perfect, monolithic control, totalitarianism obscures a great deal. Used as an ideal type describing the aims of these regimes, it still reveals something social history alone can miss.

Hannah Arendt (1951) located the novelty of both regimes in ideology joined to terror, which aimed to remake human nature. Friedrich and Brzezinski (1956) turned this into a six-point checklist. The concept was shaped by the early Cold War and could become a political weapon equating Moscow with Berlin.

Research since the 1960s exposed its limits for Germany. Broszat's The Hitler State (1969) showed overlapping, competing agencies, and Mommsen described a 'weak dictator' presiding over cumulative radicalisation. Big business, the army and the churches kept real autonomy, and the Gestapo depended heavily on denunciations from the public. For the USSR, Sheila Fitzpatrick's social historians found improvisation, local initiative and upward mobility, while the Great Terror spiralled through regional quotas and settling of scores. These findings suggest that the model, by imagining command from the top, overlooks how ordinary people took part.

Yet abandoning the concept obscures other things. The archives opened after 1991 confirmed that Stalin personally signed execution lists and that NKVD Order 00447 set quotas from the centre. Kershaw's 'working towards the Führer' reconciles chaos with Hitler's centrality. Both regimes did seek to eliminate autonomous spaces, mobilise the masses and destroy designated enemies on a scale unlike traditional dictatorships. That shared ambition is what 'totalitarian' names.

Differences remain essential. Nazism pursued racial empire and genocide; Stalinism pursued class war and forced modernisation. Their economies, party roles and fates differed. The comparative work edited by Kershaw and Lewin (1997) suggests the regimes are best compared rather than merged.

The concept therefore obscures when it implies achieved totality or identical regimes. It reveals when used heuristically, to identify an aspiration to total control whose limits historians must then explain.

questions.q: In March 1938 a fictional Foreign Office official, Arthur Penrose, writes a memorandum to the Cabinet. He argues that Britain should guarantee Czechoslovakia immediately and open military talks with France and the Soviet Union. A second official, Margaret Cole-Harding, replies that the Chiefs of Staff warn that Britain cannot fight Germany, Italy and Japan at once, that the Dominions oppose war over the Sudetenland, and that rearmament needs at least two more years. Using your knowledge of 1937–39, evaluate which official offered the more realistic policy.
markScheme: Explains the Chiefs of Staff's three-enemy warning and imperial overstretch
Dominion reluctance (e.g. South Africa, Canada) and the Imperial Conference context of 1937
Rearmament: radar and fighter priority; the 1939 RAF compared with 1938
Public opinion and economic constraints (Treasury 'fourth arm of defence')
Case for Penrose: the Czech army and fortifications, German generals' plot (Oster/Beck), Soviet treaty with Czechoslovakia (1935)
Weaknesses of the Soviet option: purged Red Army, no common border, Polish and Romanian refusal of transit
Historiographical framing: Guilty Men; revisionists (Dilks); Parker's counter-revisionism
Use of hindsight: Prague in March 1939 and the guarantee to Poland
Reaches a supported judgement
questions.modelAnswer:
Cole-Harding described the constraints of 1938 more accurately, but Penrose saw more clearly the danger of letting those constraints settle British policy.

Her case rests on solid evidence. The Chiefs of Staff warned that Britain could not fight Germany, Italy and Japan together. At the 1937 Imperial Conference and during the crisis, South Africa and Canada were reluctant to fight over the Sudetenland. Rearmament was unbalanced. Radar stations and modern fighters were only arriving, and Fighter Command was much stronger in 1939 than in 1938. The Treasury treated economic stability as a 'fourth arm of defence'. Revisionists such as David Dilks argue that these constraints left Chamberlain little choice.

Penrose's alternative has real merit. Czechoslovakia had about 35 divisions and fortifications in the Sudeten mountains. Some German generals around Beck and Oster contemplated action against Hitler if war came. The Franco-Soviet and Czech-Soviet pacts of 1935 offered a framework for an eastern front, and Parker argues Chamberlain rejected such alliances largely from distrust of Moscow.

Yet the Soviet option was weaker than it looked. The purges had devastated the Red Army's officer corps. The USSR had no border with Czechoslovakia, and Poland and Romania refused transit. France, the essential partner, was divided and defensively minded. The generals' plot is uncertain evidence on which to base policy.

Hindsight complicates the judgement. Germany gained Czech armaments and the Škoda works after March 1939, and the Nazi–Soviet Pact later removed the eastern option entirely, which makes 1938 look like a missed chance. Still, in March 1938 Cole-Harding's assessment matched the evidence available to the Cabinet. Penrose's policy was a gamble on deterrence that might have worked, but it was not the more realistic one in the circumstances.

questions.q: 'The Holocaust was the product of cumulative radicalisation rather than a long-planned programme.' Discuss.
markScheme: Defines intentionalism (Dawidowicz, Fleming) and functionalism or structuralism (Broszat, Mommsen)
Hitler's ideological antisemitism (Mein Kampf; Reichstag 'prophecy' speech, 30 January 1939)
Evolution of policy: emigration, the Madagascar plan (1940), reservations, ghettoisation
Barbarossa: Einsatzgruppen shootings escalate from men to women and children (summer–autumn 1941)
Regional initiative: Greiser in the Warthegau (Chełmno), Globocnik in Lublin
Timing debate: decision in summer, autumn or December 1941 (Browning, Gerlach); Wannsee coordinating
Synthesis: Kershaw and Longerich; ideology as necessary, war and local radicalisation as the trigger
Supported judgement
questions.modelAnswer:
The evidence supports neither a blueprint nor a story without an author. The Holocaust emerged through radicalisation, but that radicalisation was driven by Hitler's ideology.

Intentionalists such as Lucy Dawidowicz traced a line from Mein Kampf to Auschwitz. They cite Hitler's 'prophecy' in the Reichstag on 30 January 1939 that a world war would bring the annihilation of Europe's Jews. Hitler's antisemitism was obsessive and central, and without it there would have been no genocide.

Yet the path was not straight. Before 1939 policy aimed at exclusion and forced emigration. After the conquest of Poland, officials planned 'reservations' near Lublin and in 1940 considered deporting Jews to Madagascar, a plan that only made sense if mass murder had not yet been decided. Ghettos were improvised and seen as temporary.

The war against the Soviet Union transformed policy. From June 1941 the Einsatzgruppen shot Jewish men. By August and September they were killing women and children, with whole communities massacred, as at Babi Yar. Regional leaders took initiatives: Greiser's Warthegau began gassing at Chełmno in December 1941, and Globocnik developed the Operation Reinhard camps. Historians disagree on whether Hitler gave an overarching decision in late summer or autumn 1941 (Browning) or in December 1941 after the US entered the war (Gerlach). Either way, the Wannsee Conference coordinated a genocide that was already under way.

Broszat and Mommsen were right that the Nazi state's competing agencies accelerated the process. But that radicalisation always moved in the direction Hitler signalled, as Kershaw's 'working towards the Führer' explains. Longerich's synthesis presents a 'policy of annihilation' developing in stages. The Holocaust was therefore cumulative in its form and timing, and intentional in its ideological goal.

questions.q: 'The British people's war, 1939–45, created a new political consensus.' How far do you agree?
markScheme: Explains the 'people's war' interpretation (Calder 1969; Addison, The Road to 1945, 1975)
Wartime experience: evacuation revealing poverty, rationing, the Emergency Powers Act (1940), Labour ministers in the Coalition (Attlee, Bevin)
The Beveridge Report (1942) and its popularity; the 1944 Education Act; the 1944 White Paper on Employment
1945 Labour landslide; NHS (1948), nationalisation, welfare state
Challenges: Calder's later The Myth of the Blitz (1991); continuing class conflict, strikes and black market
Conservative reservations about Beveridge; Churchill's 'Gestapo' broadcast (1945)
Ben Pimlott and others questioning whether a consensus existed; 1950s Conservatives accepting the welfare state
Longer roots: interwar planning ideas (Keynes, Macmillan's The Middle Way, 1938)
Distinguishes elite policy consensus from popular attitudes
Sustained judgement
questions.modelAnswer:
The war forged a broad agreement on welfare and employment among policy elites, but calling it a 'consensus' risks hiding real conflict and longer roots.

Paul Addison's The Road to 1945 (1975) argued that the Coalition created a centre ground. Labour ministers such as Attlee and Bevin held key posts, and Whitehall accepted state planning. Evacuation exposed urban poverty to middle-class hosts. Rationing and the Emergency Powers Act of 1940 normalised intervention. The Beveridge Report (1942) sold hundreds of thousands of copies, and the 1944 Education Act and the 1944 White Paper on employment committed governments to reconstruction. Labour's landslide in 1945 and Churchill's return in 1951 without reversing the NHS suggest lasting agreement.

Several objections complicate this. Calder, author of The People's War (1969), argued in The Myth of the Blitz (1991) that wartime unity was partly constructed; looting, strikes, the black market and class resentment persisted. Conservatives were wary of Beveridge, and Churchill's 1945 claim that socialism would need a 'Gestapo' showed sharp disagreement. Pimlott dismissed consensus as a 'mirage' by pointing to fierce party conflict over nationalisation, especially of steel.

There were also prewar roots. Keynesian economics, Macmillan's The Middle Way (1938) and interwar planning movements show that ideas of a managed economy came before the war. The war gave them political opportunity rather than creating them.
